title: Hierarchical RL for Sparse-Reward Search in Commutative Algebra
one_liner: Break a hard math search into two chained steps by finding the bottleneck and constraining what moves are allowed.
lead: Standard machine learning fails on hard math problems because success is so rare — you can try thousands of moves and still not solve it. This paper treats finding counterexamples to a famous algebra conjecture as a two-phase search: first reach a special bottleneck state, then solve from there. By breaking the impossible task into steps and blocking invalid moves, the approach succeeds where standard learning fails.

problem.h2: Why math search is different from game-playing
paras: A standard AI learns by trying moves, getting reward signals (did that work?), and repeating. For chess or Go, you get feedback often: wins, losses, draws. For finding counterexamples to a mathematical conjecture, you get feedback almost never. A human might try 10,000 generator-additions and none of them produce a counterexample. The learner gets a zero reward 9,999 times and finally a signal once. That's reward sparsity.

A naive algorithm tries random moves until one works. A greedy algorithm picks the move that looks promising now. Neither strategy works here because both make the same mistake: they treat every step as equally important. Adding the right generators eventually is good, but there is an invisible bottleneck — a state structure the algorithm must pass through first. Without knowing this structure, the learner wastes effort on dead ends.
The problem is not randomness or luck. It is that the search space is huge, the goal is distant, and the path has a hidden checkpoint.

callout.html: The paper breaks sparse-reward search into two phases: reach a bottleneck state first, then solve from there, and use constraints to prune invalid moves at each phase.

panels.title: 1. Random search in chaos
panels.caption: Every move looks equally promising. No reward for thousands of steps.

panels.title: 2. Observing the winners
panels.caption: The paper watches successful attempts. They all pass through one state: the spine.

panels.title: 3. Phase 1: Reach the spine
panels.caption: First option narrows moves to those heading toward the bottleneck. No wasted drift.

panels.title: 4. Phase 2: Linearize from spine
panels.caption: Second option knows the starting point. Only valid algebraic moves allowed.

panels.title: 5. Success: two-phase route
panels.caption: Breaking the task into steps with constraints recovers solutions the learner missed.

steps.text: Train on a small set of solved examples; note which states appear in every solution path.
The spine is the bottleneck state structure all solutions pass through.
Learn a policy that reaches the spine, with hard constraints blocking moves away from it.
Learn a policy that solves from the spine, constrained to only valid algebraic moves.
Execute phase 1, then phase 2; the two-step structure now solves problems end-to-end.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the action mask
paras: Standard RL lets the learner try any move from any state. This paper changes the set of allowed moves at each state by using hard constraints: a mask that flags which actions are invalid and blocks them before the learner even attempts them.

The mask is different in each phase: phase 1 masks everything that doesn't lead to the spine, phase 2 masks everything that violates algebraic rules. The object being changed is the action mask (a binary flag for each possible move).

hidden.name: Bottleneck state frequency
paras: The paper measures an invisible quantity: how often does a particular state appear in successful solution paths? If the state appears in 95% of successful trajectories, it is a true bottleneck. If it appears in 5%, it is noise.

The paper estimates this by training a standard agent on a small set of examples, collecting trajectories that reach the goal, and counting state visits. High-frequency states are candidate spines. The spine is the state where the paper draws the phase boundary.

heat.caption: Darker means the state appears more often in successful paths. The spine (bottleneck) is visited by almost all solutions.

reads.html: A spine is a state that all successful solution paths must pass through. Finding it reveals the hidden structure of the problem.
The paper identifies spines by analyzing high-probability paths in successful trajectories and confirms their necessity via counterfactual removal.

mechanism.h2: Why constraining the search into two phases works
paras: Standard RL explores blindly because it has no structure. The learner is like a person in a maze with no map, trying random hallways. It eventually succeeds but wastes enormous effort.

The paper's insight is that hard math problems have invisible structure: a bottleneck. Once you identify this bottleneck empirically (by watching what works), you can exploit it. Instead of learning one long policy, the paper learns two shorter policies, each with constraints that block invalid moves. Phase 1 learns to reach the bottleneck; phase 2 learns to finish from there.

The payoff is dramatic: both phases are now shorter, simpler problems. The learner spends no energy on moves that go the wrong direction (phase 1 blocks them), and no energy on moves that violate algebra rules (phase 2 blocks them). The action space shrinks, the path to the goal becomes clearer, and learning succeeds. The paper proves this via an equivariant graph neural policy, which respects the symmetry of the algebra: if two generator-sets are algebraically equivalent, the policy treats them the same way. This symmetry awareness further speeds learning.

stages.s: Graph neural network encodes the ideal as node/edge features
Phase 1: constrained policy (reach spine) with action mask
Phase 2: constrained policy (solve from spine) with action mask

math.words: For each option (phase), a hard constraint masks invalid actions before the learner sees them. The reward is a fixed penalty per step (negative one) until the goal is reached, ensuring the learner finds short paths. A hard mask applied to the policy output sets invalid actions to very large negative values, forcing the learner to ignore them.
math.equation: r(s, a, s') = -1 (cost per step);  logits_masked[a] = logits[a] if a in C(s) else -infinity;  policy = softmax(logits_masked)
symbols: reward for taking action a from state s to next state s'
set of constrained valid actions at state s
raw network score for action a before masking
network score after applying the hard constraint mask
cost for each step (encourages short solutions)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: State S (5 generators): policy outputs raw scores [0.2, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.4].
Constraint C(S) says actions 0, 2, 4 are valid (move toward spine).
Hard mask sets invalid actions to -1e9: logits_masked = [0.2, -1e9, 0.3, -1e9, 0.4].
Softmax converts to probabilities [0.25, 0, 0.35, 0, 0.40] (valid actions only).
Learner now only tries moves 0, 2, 4. Moves 1, 3 have zero chance, no wasted exploration.

math.note: Hard masking forces the policy to respect structure; the learner never wastes steps on forbidden moves.

bars.h2: What improves: success rate and step efficiency

charts.title: Standard RL (no constraints)
charts.note: Standard learner tries random moves, rarely succeeds.

charts.title: This paper (two-phase constrained HRL)
charts.note: Two phases with hard constraints prune the search and consistently find solutions.

items.html: If the identified bottleneck is not actually a necessary waypoint, phase 1 may force the learner away from all solutions. The paper verifies spines by checking that removing them blocks all solutions in the training set.

If phase 2 blocks too many algebraic moves, the learner cannot reach any goal from the spine. The paper uses both hard constraints (guaranteed to preserve all solutions) and soft constraints (gentle nudging) to balance.

A standard neural network can fail to respect algebraic symmetry, leading to poor generalization across different generator sets. The paper uses an equivariant graph neural network (syzygy-aware message passing) to handle this.

The paper verifies that spines are necessary, constrains are sufficient (solutions still reachable), and the graph network learns symmetries, so the approach generalizes across problem sizes and degrees.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo generates a random commutative algebra problem (5–10 generators, degree 3–4), trains a standard end-to-end RL agent and a two-phase constrained HRL agent on the same budget (10,000 steps each), and counts how many times each agent finds a non-Hirsch ideal. Measure also the average number of steps needed for successful runs.
demo.metric_eq: Success rate = (number of problems solved) / (total problems); Efficiency = average steps per solved problem
demo.closing: The demo must show that constraining the search into two phases with hard action masks increases success rate and reduces wasted exploration relative to standard RL.
